--- title: "Championships: NBA and WNBA eras" --- ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"} ## Why the time windows differ - **NBA section:** **2005-06 to 2025-26**, starting with the first season that has salaries reported for about 99% of minutes. - **WNBA section:** every WNBA season we have, **2009 to 2026**. WNBA salary records start only in 2021, and starting there would leave six champions to learn from. - **NBA vs WNBA:** the two leagues are compared season against season, never pooled. - **Models that learn from champions use all of each league's seasons in its window.** There is one champion per season, so a short window leaves too few champions to test a model. - **Shot zones are calibrated by season.** ESPN's recorded shot positions drift between eras, most visibly in the WNBA's 2020 bubble season, so the rim zone is anchored to where layups are recorded each season (Data page). ::: ::: {#takeaways .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Takeaways - **NBA playoffs punish threes and rim attempts.** Points per three fell in the playoffs in 100% of NBA seasons since 2005-06 (-0.040 per shot); rim attempts in 90%. Mid-range shots held up best. - **WNBA playoffs:** no shot zone shows a reliable playoff change; with 8-12 playoff teams a year the sample is small. - **WNBA 2026's shot mix most resembles the NBA in 2018-19** on three-point share, which points to which NBA champions to study (below). - **Recent champions vs their own league (2022-26):** WNBA champions +5.3 points of shots from three and -6.3 at the rim; NBA champions +2.3 and -0.7. - **Net rating plus our availability-adjusted strength predicts NBA playoff series better than net rating alone** (74% vs 70% called correctly). ::: ::: # NBA (2005-06 to 2025-26) ## NBA: which shots survive the playoffs? ```{=html}
``` **What this shows:** bars left of zero are shots that get worse in the playoffs; the whiskers are 95% intervals. In the NBA, three, rim, paint / short mid, long mid reliably lose value, with **three** losing the most (-0.040 points per shot, worse in 100% of seasons). Shots that cross zero hold up about as well as in the regular season. ## NBA: champion identity ```{=html}
``` **What this shows:** each dot is an NBA champion. Right = better offense than the league that season, up = better defense. A champion is *offense-led* when its offensive edge beats its defensive edge by 3+ points per 100 possessions, *defense-led* the reverse, otherwise *balanced*. Of 21 NBA champions, 14 were balanced, 4 offense-led and 3 defense-led (these are counts of teams). Recent champions: GS 2022: defense-led; DEN 2023: balanced; BOS 2024: offense-led; OKC 2025: balanced; NY 2026: balanced. **How to read these tables:** every number is the champions' average minus the league average that season, in percentage points of team minutes or shots. +5 means the champions gave 5 points more of their minutes (or shots) to that role than the average team did; 0 means they looked like everyone else. *Champions* is the number of title teams in that era. Positions are the listed G / F / C; archetypes describe how players actually play, so a team can have few centers but many interior roles, or the reverse. **How NBA champions' shots differed from the league** (percentage points; + = more of that shot than the league) | era | champions | threes | rim | mid-range | assisted makes | |:--------|------------:|---------:|------:|------------:|-----------------:| | 2006-10 | 5 | 1.7 | -0.2 | -1.5 | 0.8 | | 2011-16 | 6 | 2.9 | -0.9 | -2 | 2.4 | | 2017-21 | 5 | 1 | 0.2 | -1.2 | 3.9 | | 2022-26 | 5 | 2.3 | -0.7 | -1.6 | 1.4 | **NBA champions' archetype minutes minus the league average** (percentage points) | era | Connector forward | Hub big / point forward | On-ball creator | Rim-running big | Secondary guard | Spot-up 3-and-D wing | |:--------|--------------------:|--------------------------:|------------------:|------------------:|------------------:|-----------------------:| | 2006-10 | -2.8 | -0.5 | 0.8 | -1 | -1.9 | 5.4 | | 2011-16 | -6.3 | -3.8 | 0.5 | 0.8 | 2.4 | 6.4 | | 2017-21 | -3.5 | 3.1 | -2.1 | -0.2 | -2.9 | 5.7 | | 2022-26 | -0.6 | -2 | -1.6 | -2.2 | 0.4 | 6 | **NBA champions' minutes by listed position, minus the league average** (percentage points) | era | champions | guards | forwards | centers | |:--------|------------:|---------:|-----------:|----------:| | 2006-10 | 5 | -4.4 | 5.5 | -1.1 | | 2011-16 | 6 | 3.1 | -2.2 | -0.9 | | 2017-21 | 5 | -4.4 | 9.2 | -4.8 | | 2022-26 | 5 | 6.7 | -7.7 | 1.1 | **Team composition, era by era:** - **2006-10** (5 champions): most extra minutes to **Spot-up 3-and-D wing** (+5.4 points vs the league), fewest to **Connector forward** (-2.8); by listed position, forwards got the most extra minutes (+5.5). - **2011-16** (6 champions): most extra minutes to **Spot-up 3-and-D wing** (+6.4 points vs the league), fewest to **Connector forward** (-6.3); by listed position, guards got the most extra minutes (+3.1). - **2017-21** (5 champions): most extra minutes to **Spot-up 3-and-D wing** (+5.7 points vs the league), fewest to **Connector forward** (-3.5); by listed position, forwards got the most extra minutes (+9.2). - **2022-26** (5 champions): most extra minutes to **Spot-up 3-and-D wing** (+6.0 points vs the league), fewest to **Rim-running big** (-2.2); by listed position, guards got the most extra minutes (+6.7). ## NBA: picking champions and series Trained season by season on earlier seasons only, with recent seasons weighted more (the weighting is chosen from past seasons, never the one being predicted). | model | avg chance given to the eventual champion | champion in top 3 | playoff series called correctly | |:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:--------------------|:----------------------------------| | net rating only (reference) | 15% | 54% | 70% | | availability-adjusted strength only | 15% | 77% | 74% | | net rating + availability-adjusted strength | 18% | 69% | 74% | | net + availability-adjusted (offense, defense) + archetype x quality + age | 15% | 69% | 71% | **What this shows:** *net rating* is the team's points scored minus allowed per 100 possessions. *Availability-adjusted strength* is our variable: the team rebuilt from this season's lineup-based player impact, counting only the players available for the playoffs. Combined, our variable carries **51% of the model's weight** against 49% for net rating. Over every NBA playoff series, adding it to net rating improves predictions (+0.020 log-likelihood per series, one-sided p = 0.03). # WNBA (2009 to 2026) ## WNBA: which shots survive the playoffs? ```{=html}
``` **What this shows:** no WNBA shot zone has a reliable playoff change; every interval crosses zero. With few playoff teams each year the {lg} sample is small, so the honest reading is 'no clear penalty yet'. ## WNBA: champion identity ```{=html}
``` **What this shows:** each dot is a WNBA champion. Right = better offense than the league that season, up = better defense. by listed position, centers got the most extra minutes (+2.0). ## WNBA: picking champions and series The WNBA has 12-15 teams, so a random pick already has a 7-12% chance; every number here comes from 10 or fewer test seasons. | model | avg chance given to the eventual champion | champion in top 3 | playoff series called correctly | |:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:--------------------|:----------------------------------| | net rating only (reference) | 30% | 80% | 71% | | availability-adjusted strength only | 27% | 80% | 70% | | net rating + availability-adjusted strength | 35% | 80% | 71% | | net + availability-adjusted (offense, defense) + archetype x quality + age | 37% | 80% | 70% | **What this shows:** *net rating* is the team's points scored minus allowed per 100 possessions. *Availability-adjusted strength* is our variable: the team rebuilt from this season's lineup-based player impact, counting only the players available for the playoffs. Combined, our variable carries **45% of the model's weight** against 55% for net rating. Over every WNBA playoff series, adding it to net rating improves predictions (+0.008 log-likelihood per series, one-sided p = 0.05). # NBA vs WNBA: which NBA season does each WNBA season resemble? This is not a measure of one league being "behind" the other. For each WNBA season, it finds the NBA season whose shot mix is the same, so we can look at what won in that NBA season and ask whether the same patterns show up in the WNBA. ```{=html}
``` | WNBA season | closest NBA season | NBA champion then | WNBA champion | |--------------:|:---------------------|:--------------------|:------------------| | 2019 | 2015-16 | CLE (balanced) | WSH (offense-led) | | 2020 | 2016-17 | GS (balanced) | SEA (defense-led) | | 2021 | 2016-17 | GS (balanced) | CHI (balanced) | | 2022 | 2017-18 | GS (offense-led) | LV (offense-led) | | 2023 | 2016-17 | GS (balanced) | LV (offense-led) | | 2024 | 2017-18 | GS (offense-led) | NY (balanced) | | 2025 | 2018-19 | TOR (balanced) | LV (balanced) | | 2026 | 2019-20 | LAL (balanced) | GS (defense-led) | **What this shows:** both lines rise together: as the WNBA has taken more threes and fewer mid-range shots, the NBA season it resembles has moved forward too, and by 2026 it matches the NBA of about 2019-20 on threes. The table pairs each recent WNBA season with its closest NBA season and both champions. Where the identities line up (for example balanced champions in both), the NBA's later seasons are a reasonable guide to what the WNBA may reward next; where they differ, the WNBA is following its own path. ## Shot mix, both leagues ```{=html}
``` **What this shows:** both leagues are moving the same direction (more threes, fewer mid-range shots), the NBA earlier and faster. The WNBA's mid-range share has fallen most since 2020. ::: {.caveat} Association, not causation. Each league is measured against itself; NBA and WNBA numbers are compared, never pooled. :::
